articles.full_text:
Conclusion

This analysis examined a campaign that abuses exposed Microsoft SQL Server instances to deliver additional malware. The payload, a UPX-packed Go binary that uses the Naabu scanner, retrieves a target IP range from its C2 server, probes TCP port 1433 to identify reachable servers, and records each successful response in Result.txt.

The downloaded go.vbs starts go.bat, which launches dwm.exe to brute-force MSSQL logins using a predefined list of users and passwords. It then executes the T-SQL commands in 2018.sql on each compromised server. Those commands enable xp_cmdshell and download or extract a loader into C:\Users\Public. The loader, in turn, pulls additional malicious executables from an FTP server.

During my analysis, malware samples were downloaded: “MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe” is an XMRig miner that uses the compromised server's CPU to mine Monero; “winlogon.exe” is a Gh0st RAT that provides keylogging, screen capture, file management, a remote shell, and more than 30 control commands for remotely controlling the compromised MS SQL servers.

Fortinet Protections

Fortinet customers are already protected from this campaign with FortiGuard’s IPS, Web Filtering, and AntiVirus services as follows:

The domains and URLs associated with this campaign are rated as Malicious Websites by the FortiGuard Web Filtering service.

FortiGuard Antivirus detects the malicious files described in this report with the following AV signatures:

W64/MSSQLBruteforcer.F62C!tr W64/Agent.DRN!tr W32/Agent.DAV!tr VBS/Agent.PPWT!tr MSIL/Agent.AFL!tr …

FortiGuard IPS signature MS.SQL.Server.Brute.Force.Login detects brute force attacks against Microsoft SQL Server.

FortiGates detect port scan by enabling tcp_port_scan in the DoS policy.

Fortinet FortiGate, FortiMail, FortiClient, and FortiEDR support the FortiGuard AntiVirus service, and each solution includes the FortiGuard AntiVirus engine. As a result, customers using these products already have up-to-date protections.

To stay informed of new and emerging threats, sign up to receive future alerts.

We also suggest that our readers complete the free NSE training: NSE 1 – Information Security Awareness, which includes information on Internet threats and is designed to help end users identify and protect themselves against phishing attacks.

The FortiPhish Phishing Simulation Service, together with Fortinet’s Security Awareness and Training Service, uses real-world phishing scenarios to train and test employees against common social engineering tactics. By improving users’ ability to recognize and respond to suspicious content—especially during high-risk periods of distraction or urgency—these services help reduce the risk of successful phishing and malware attacks.

If you believe this or any other cybersecurity threat has impacted your organization, please contact our Global FortiGuard Incident Response Team.

articles.title: Beyond the Kill Switch: Containing AI Agents at Machine Speed
articles.context: Fortinet and FortiGuard Labs bring critical threat research and operational experience to that effort, helping identify suspicious patterns in tool use and data access and...
articles.full_text:
AI agents can retrieve information, use tools, and trigger actions across multiple systems before a security team can assess their decisions. If an agent begins operating outside its authorized purpose, the organization must immediately contain the risk and determine which parts of the business process can safely continue. However, harmful actions unfold faster than human defenders can respond.

Closing this gap is a focus of Fortinet’s recent contributions to the World Economic Forum Centre for Cybersecurity’s Cyber Frontiers: AI and Cybersecurity initiative. Fortinet’s participation includes an in-person meeting in San Francisco last month and ongoing initiative workshops. Through this collaboration, we bring a practitioner’s perspective on translating agent governance into enforceable controls.

Effective containment requires AI-enabled security that detects signs of misuse and automatically triggers controls to restrict an agent’s actions. Enforcement must extend beyond prompts to the agent’s tools, credentials, active context, and stored memory. These controls must also give security teams time to assess an incident and choose an appropriate response. An agent kill switch remains an essential last resort when narrower interventions cannot reliably contain the risk. However, it must be designed to support business continuity, allowing it to stop an affected agent while safe, authorized work continues.

Here are critical steps every organization can take to secure their AI agent deployments:

1. Establish What an Agent Is Allowed to Do

Detecting misuse begins with a clear understanding of an AI agent’s legitimate role. Before deployment, organizations must define the agent’s identity, purpose, accountable owner, and authorized scope. This scope needs to specify which tools it can invoke, what information it can access, and which actions it can delegate.

With those boundaries established, AI-enabled monitoring can assess whether an agent’s activity remains consistent with its assigned task. That assessment must go beyond checking credentials: An agent using valid credentials and permitted tools can still request an inappropriate operation or access information unrelated to its purpose.

When monitoring detects a deviation, the first priority is to limit potential harm. Whether the cause is a compromise, faulty instructions, or a routine error, containment must begin before the uncertainty is resolved. Predefined intervention criteria should specify which actions to block, which permissions to restrict, and which cases require human review.

Defining those criteria beforehand requires an understanding of both attack behavior and legitimate operations. Fortinet and FortiGuard Labs bring critical threat research and operational experience to that effort, helping identify suspicious patterns in tool use and data access and linking those signals to proportionate controls.

2. Use Deception to Strengthen Detection

Deception techniques can generate useful detection signals. Fortinet’s deception technologies include deploying decoy assets and credentials to identify credential misuse and lateral movement. Agentic workflows can build on this approach: A canary credential or decoy tool outside an agent’s authorized task, for example, could reveal an attempt to exceed its scope. That signal could trigger a targeted restriction or pause while a person assesses the situation.

For threat researchers, the key question is how reliably these techniques translate into agent behavior. Testing should determine how to interpret the signal in context—including benign discovery and configuration errors—and what response is warranted. Agent-specific applications should also be validated before organizations rely on them for containment.

3. Contain Risk While Preserving Verified Work

Responses must address both potential harm and whatever remains trustworthy. Consider a hypothetical security operations agent investigating suspicious activity. If the agent recommends isolating a production system without verifying its business dependencies, acting on that recommendation could cause as much harm as the threat it is intended to contain.

Unless a preapproved containment policy authorizes an action, an approval gate should pause the isolation request before execution. This gives an analyst time to assess potential operational consequences. Authorized evidence collection can continue as long as the process remains secure and appropriately restricted. If the agent’s identity or working context may be compromised, move supporting work to a trusted process or analyst using trusted tools, and treat suspect evidence as untrusted data.

Graduated containment provides several ways to make that distinction operational:

Throttle authorized activity. Limit tool-call rates, concurrent tasks, execution time, and the number of retries or delegated steps. This constrains automation loops and creates time to investigate. Unauthorized actions or imminent harm require an immediate block or stronger containment.

Restrict permissions and connectivity. Remove write access, disable specific tools, or limit network destinations. Use task-scoped credentials with short lifetimes so you can withdraw authority without disrupting unrelated services. Read-only access also warrants scrutiny when sensitive information could be transmitted elsewhere.

Limit active context. The context window contains the instructions, history, and retrieved content supplied to the model for its next decision. The application can cap how much task data enters that window and restrict retrieval to approved sources. If context may be poisoned, preserve a snapshot and rebuild it from a trusted task definition and validated state. Simply shortening the window is insufficient: It can discard necessary instructions while leaving malicious content in place.

Restrict persistent memory. Stored conversation history, summaries, and retrieval records can influence later decisions. Limit the records an agent can read or write, separate memory by task or user, apply expiration rules, and quarantine suspect entries. Clearing active context does not remove poisoned persistent memory, and neither operation revokes the agent’s tool permissions.

Require additional approval. Hold higher-risk actions for review by an authorized person. Bind approval to the specific operation, target, parameters, and scope. A material change should require another decision.

Pause or isolate the affected work. Suspend the agent or a workflow branch, preserve evidence, and keep suspect outputs from reaching downstream systems. Continue other work only when its dependencies and controls can be independently validated; treat evidence from suspect sources as untrusted data.

These options can be combined according to the incident. They are not a mandatory sequence: Active compromise or imminent harm may warrant an immediate stop.

4. Enforce Limits Where Agents Act

A gateway model offers a practical way to enforce these restrictions. Agent requests to models, tools, APIs, and services must pass through control points that evaluate them before execution. A policy decision point then determines whether a request is allowed, requires approval, or must be denied. An enforcement point at the gateway, tool executor, or receiving service enforces that decision. Both must operate outside the acting agent’s authority.

Agent-aware enforcement should link each request to an identifiable agent, an accountable owner, a delegated task, and an authorized scope. It should evaluate the operation and its parameters, the destination, the resource’s sensitivity, and any delegation involved. In the security operations example above, this means setting separate authorization requirements for evidence collection and production isolation.

AI guardrails can inspect prompts, retrieved content, responses, and proposed tool calls for signs of injection, data leakage, or other policy violations. Tool authorization must still independently verify which actions are permitted. An agent’s claim that an action is safe or that approval has been granted does not constitute authorization. If required approval or policy checks fail, the affected high-risk action should remain blocked.

The architecture must also account for bypass paths. Blocking a single connector is ineffective if an agent can access the same function through another tool or delegate the task to an unrestricted agent. You must cover all relevant execution paths and verify authorization in the systems receiving requests. The agent application and storage controls should also manage context and memory restrictions; a gateway alone cannot enforce every aspect of the workflow.

This separation aligns with OWASP’s AI Agent Security guidance, which recommends enforcing authorization outside the agent’s context, validating approvals for specific tool calls, and isolating and limiting memory.

Fortinet’s work on AI security reflects this architecture. FortiAIGate provides a runtime gateway with guardrails for prompts, responses, and agent tool traffic and adds automated AI validation, agent security, and real-time protection. These capabilities support independent inspection and policy enforcement. Organizations must also implement the task-specific permissions, memory controls, and continuity procedures described here.

5. Define Human Decisions Before an Incident

Automated enforcement enables timely intervention, but humans must still define the policies that govern it. Before deployment, teams should agree on which signals trigger restrictions, who can intervene, and when an incident calls for escalation or a complete stop.

Higher-risk actions that require approval should remain blocked until a decision is made. Escalation deadlines and safe fallback procedures should account for situations where no reviewer is available. Organizations should also test whether their staffing and escalation processes can handle the volume of decisions generated by agents.

Reviewers also need evidence to support a decision: what the agent attempted to do, which actions it completed, which restrictions are in effect, and which systems or data may be affected. Without that context, an alert can leave someone responsible for a decision they’re not equipped to make.

6. Design Your Emergency Kill Switch for Business Continuity

An emergency stop should revoke the suspect agent’s authority while preserving the underlying business process wherever it remains safe. This includes halting the affected run through the orchestration layer, revoking its task credentials and sessions, and propagating restrictions to child agents and delegated jobs. You should also block new tool calls at external enforcement points and cancel queued work. In-flight operations require explicit handling: cancel them where supported, determine what has already completed, and reconcile or compensate for completed changes where possible.

Continuity depends on having a tested fallback in place in advance. Keep unfinished work in a protected queue, and hand validated tasks to an analyst, a constrained playbook, or an independently trusted service. For example, a SOC can keep receiving and routing alerts while suspending the suspect agent’s response privileges. The fallback must not automatically inherit the same compromised context, memory, or credentials.

Keep checkpoints and action records outside the agent’s control so a replacement agent or analyst can distinguish completed actions from pending work and reduce the risk of duplicate execution. These records support a controlled handoff, but continuity also requires a tested fallback. A kill switch alone cannot keep the business process running safely. If no safe fallback exists, the affected process may need to be paused.

Before an agent resumes, responders should verify affected systems, address the root cause of the incident, and validate a trusted configuration, context, and memory state. A designated person should authorize restoration, and permissions should be returned incrementally where appropriate. Exercises should test the entire workflow, including revocation, delegated tasks, fallback operations, and safe resumption.

Turn Collaboration into Operational Guidance

Implementing such controls requires cooperation across the agentic ecosystem. Enterprises rely on model developers and tool providers for visibility and enforceable boundaries. Security researchers need operational feedback to evaluate detection methods. Policymakers need to understand where technical controls can support accountability and where gaps remain.

Cyber Frontiers brings together public- and private-sector perspectives on securing agentic AI. Through our participation, we share Fortinet’s operational experience while learning from organizations with systems, constraints, and consequences of failure that differ from our own. Comparing approaches helps clarify responsibilities and assess whether proposed safeguards can work when agents interact across organizational boundaries.

The practical value comes from sharing what organizations learn when those safeguards are tested: which observations warranted intervention, how quickly restrictions took effect, whether delegated tasks were halted, and what enabled safe operations to continue. Organizations can apply these lessons to test their own workflows before expanding agent autonomy. Those tests should demonstrate that controls can detect misuse, apply proportionate restrictions, and give an accountable person the evidence and authority to decide what happens next.

Learn more about the forum’s Cyber Frontiers initiative and its work to support secure adoption across the agentic economy.

articles.title: Omdia Quantifies the Business Value of Fortinet Unified SASE
articles.context: Explore Omdia’s economic validation of Fortinet Unified SASE, including modeled cost savings, operational efficiencies, and improved user productivity.
articles.full_text:
The business case for secure access service edge (SASE) hinges on how well it integrates networking and security. Organizations that manage separate SD-WAN and security service edge (SSE) products alongside legacy VPNs may still contend with fragmented policies, multiple consoles, and substantial integration work. These operational costs can reduce the value of convergence.

A new Omdia Economic Validation report, The Economic Benefits of Fortinet Unified SASE (October 2026), examines the financial impact of a unified approach. Commissioned by Fortinet, Omdia interviewed customers in education, government, and healthcare—three sectors with tight budgets, distributed users, and strict compliance requirements—and developed an economic model based on their experiences. The findings connect lower infrastructure costs with reduced administrative effort and improved employee productivity.

The Three-Year Financial Model

Omdia used its interview findings to model a composite enterprise with approximately 50,000 employees, 500 locations, and 20,000 remote or hybrid workers. This model’s initial environment included costly WAN connections, multiple security products, and traditional VPN access. The model estimates the following over three years:

Approximately $50.1 million in benefits against $8.4 million invested, yielding $41.6 million in net value and a 493% return on investment

A 47% reduction in total cost of ownership (TCO) for networking, security, and operations

A 59% reduction in time spent managing and supporting operations, saving more than 21,000 hours

Payback within the first year, with approximately $13 million in first-year cumulative benefits against $3.5 million invested

These modeled results offer a framework for evaluating a SASE investment. Actual returns will depend on an organization’s existing infrastructure, connectivity costs, staffing, and deployment scope.

Reducing the Work of Managing Separate Systems

The 59% reduction in operational effort helps explain how the modeled returns are achieved. Fortinet Unified SASE unifies the SD-WAN edge and cloud-delivered SSE on a common FortiOS operating system, with unified management and a shared data lake. This architecture enables teams apply consistent policies and investigate issues without switching between disconnected tools.

Customer interviews illustrate the practical impact. General network and security administration produced the greatest absolute time savings. Remote access management became simpler when zero-trust network access replaced legacy VPN deployments. One customer cut the time to bring a site online from about a month to just days, and reduced acquisition integration from as long as three months to about three to four weeks.

Customers also reported that a single console made compliance reporting simpler. For organizations in regulated sectors, spending less time gathering and reconciling information can free staff to focus on other security and operational priorities.

Vendor and platform consolidation accounts for another 12% of modeled benefits by reducing licenses, simplifying procurement, and decreasing the number of vendor relationships to manage. Faster integration also helps acquired organizations start using shared systems sooner.

Improving Productivity and Resilience

End-user productivity accounts for 25% of modeled benefits. One healthcare customer reported that doctors had previously lost reliable connectivity after about three hours of work; deployment resolved the issue. Education customers reported fewer connectivity complaints from users on campus, at home, and while traveling.

Improved resilience contributes an additional 11% to the modeled benefits. One customer replaced a single internet connection with two connections and SD-WAN failover. For a clinic or school that depends on continuous application access, this can reduce disruption if a connection fails.

Supporting AI Adoption with Consistent Controls

The report also frames these findings against rising infrastructure demands. Omdia survey data cited in the report show that 80% of organizations are investing in AI infrastructure, while 69% say their environments have grown more complex over the past two years.

One interviewee described a related visibility issue: Before deployment, the organization didn’t know who was using AI tools or what data employees were entering into them. Consolidating generative AI access security, data loss prevention, and cloud access security broker capabilities together on one platform helps teams govern usage and protect sensitive information. These controls are especially relevant in government and healthcare, where employees handle regulated data.

Using Connectivity Savings to Support Modernization

Network and security cost optimization represents the largest category of benefits in Omdia’s model. One customer replaced MPLS circuits that cost roughly $2,000 with cable connections costing about $150, while gaining more than 30 times the bandwidth.

Savings at that scale can help fund broader modernization. By pairing connectivity changes with networking and security consolidation, organizations can assess the transition's costs alongside the operational and security benefits of the resulting architecture.

Applying These Findings to Your Organization

While the composite enterprise is large, the issues it addresses also affect smaller organizations. A small IT team managing multiple consoles and contracts can benefit from consolidation, and connectivity costs can be evaluated on a per-site basis. The study’s percentage reductions provide useful benchmarks for that assessment, though smaller organizations should not assume equivalent returns.

The next step is to build a business case using your organization’s cost data. Compare current circuit and licensing expenses, factor in the time spent managing separate systems, and include migration and deployment costs. A proof of concept can then validate operational improvements and the user experience before a broader rollout.

articles.context: Conclusion This malware is not “garage” or student-level work
articles.full_text:
Game Server Communication

All communication with the game servers is authenticated and encrypted. The AES encryption key is included in the /srvlist response from the line configuration servers (field aes_key). For authentication, all requests are signed with HMAC-SHA256, a keyed hash message authentication code that computes the hash of a message and a shared secret (the AES key in our case).

Because the AES key is returned in cleartext from the line config servers, the purpose is not to address confidentiality or integrity against a third party, but rather to obfuscate content and check for communication errors.

Conclusion

This malware is not “garage” or student-level work. It reflects well-planned development, with a clean infrastructure, multiple REST APIs, and a full ecosystem. In 2024, with limited reverse engineering tooling, this Flutter application would have taken ages to reverse engineer. In 2026, however, it’s merely a hard day’s work. It’s always good news to hear that cybercriminals are losing their edge.

Cybersecurity is constantly changing, and so are the skills IT professionals need to protect their organizations. As the cybersecurity workforce continues to evolve, access to relevant training, recognized credentials, and opportunities to build practical skills has become increasingly important.

For more than a decade, the Fortinet Training Institute has expanded people’s easy access to cybersecurity education and career development. Fortinet has fulfilled its pledge to train 1 million people in cybersecurity months ahead of schedule.

This achievement is one measure of the Fortinet Training Institute’s success. Industry recognition offers another perspective, highlighting programs and approaches across professional certification, cybersecurity education, and security awareness.

articles.title: Cyber Resilience Starts with AI Governance
articles.context: It can improve operational efficiency and enable faster threat detection and response
articles.full_text:
Today’s cybercriminals are increasingly using AI to scale, accelerate, and evolve their attacks. At the same time, organizations are recognizing that AI can be a powerful force for defense, using it to strengthen cybersecurity, improve security operations, and protect networks at machine speed.

Data in the Fortinet 2026 Cybersecurity Skills Gap Report confirms the near-ubiquity of this response, with 91% of the IT leaders in the 2,700+ organizations surveyed stating they are using or exploring the use of AI-empowered cybersecurity solutions. Unfortunately, as we move higher up the corporate ladder, only 50% of respondents believe their boards of directors fully comprehend the cybersecurity vulnerabilities associated with AI. This disconnect highlights a governance gap, which creates risk for the organization.

Why Boards of Directors Need to Fully Understand AI

To defend against AI-powered criminals, organizations need to build cyber resilience, but they can’t do that if leadership doesn't understand AI and its potential risks. That gap becomes even more significant as AI-driven defenses become more embedded within organizations. As AI adoption accelerates, company-wide AI literacy and cybersecurity governance must evolve alongside it.

According to the Fortinet 2026 Cybersecurity Skills Gap Report, although nearly three-quarters of respondents say their boards view cybersecurity as a business priority, only 59% say that priority is reflected in spending decisions. This discrepancy suggests many organizations recognize the importance of cybersecurity in principle but struggle to translate that awareness into sustained investment and governance.

The report also highlights what's at stake for leadership. Half of organizations say board members or senior executives faced personal consequences following a cyberattack, including fines, loss of employment, or other penalties. As cyber risk increasingly becomes business risk, executive oversight has never been more important.

AI-Informed Leadership Teams

Board members don’t need to become AI engineers. But they do need enough understanding of AI to ask the right questions, evaluate risk, and provide effective oversight.

AI literacy also shouldn’t stop with the boardroom or the security team. IT staff, software developers, and business leaders also need a foundational understanding of how AI systems work, the risks they pose, and how to mitigate those risks.

For boards and C-suite leaders, education should focus on governance, risk oversight, executive accountability, policies, investment decisions, and regulatory implications. With a shared knowledge base across the organization, leaders can better balance the productivity and security benefits of AI with its potential risks.

The goal is an AI-informed leadership team that can balance AI's potential with its risks and make informed decisions about adoption, investment, and governance.

What Should Organizations Do Today to Build AI Literacy?

Organizations should begin by assessing their current AI readiness and identifying knowledge gaps across leadership, security teams, IT, and the broader workforce.

An organization’s board of directors must understand the benefits that come with AI adoption. First, AI can act as a force multiplier for short-handed IT security teams. It can improve operational efficiency and enable faster threat detection and response. But leadership must also recognize that realizing these benefits requires people with the skills to securely manage, oversee, and govern AI-enabled environments.

Organizations can address these challenges through a combination of governance, workforce education, and structured skills development. Programs that provide AI education and cybersecurity certification can help employees build the knowledge needed to use, secure, and responsibly manage AI.

The Fortinet Training Institute can help your organization acquire AI literacy and workforce education. Training programs are designed to support the acquisition of technical expertise across leadership, security teams, and the broader workforce.

AI is already changing how organizations defend themselves. The next step is ensuring the people responsible for guiding that transformation understand both its opportunities and its risks.

As organizations strengthen AI governance, another workforce challenge comes into focus: finding and developing professionals with the skills to secure, manage, and govern increasingly AI-enabled environments.

Need more guidance on how to educate the board on AI? Explore Fortinet Training Institute programs and certification pathways to learn how Fortinet is helping close the cyber skills gap through accessible training, upskilling, reskilling, and workforce development.

articles.title: Simplify Operations and Strengthen Protection with Fortinet AI-Driven Secure SD-WAN
articles.context: Learn how Fortinet AI-Driven Secure SD-WAN simplifies operations, improves application performance, and strengthens protection across distributed networks.
articles.full_text:
IT teams managing distributed networks face growing pressure to deliver reliable application experiences while protecting an expanding attack surface. Cloud adoption and generative AI (GenAI) are increasing demands on the WAN, while shadow AI, the use of unsanctioned AI applications and services, creates visibility, data protection, and governance challenges. Emerging technologies such as quantum computing also pose long-term risks to data confidentiality. Manual troubleshooting and fragmented visibility make it harder to address these challenges and keep pace with business requirements.

When application performance degrades, determining the cause can require extensive investigation. Teams must examine WAN conditions, overlay connectivity, routing, and security policies, often across multiple locations. Routine configuration changes add to the workload, consuming resources that could otherwise support strategic business initiatives.

Fortinet AI-Driven Secure SD-WAN addresses these challenges by converging intelligent networking, AI-powered security, and automation on a unified platform. Built on FortiGate firewalls and the FortiOS operating system and accelerated by purpose-built ASICs, it helps organizations simplify operations, strengthen protection, and improve application performance while mitigating emerging AI and cryptographic risks.

Accelerate Troubleshooting and Streamline Network Operations

Resolving connectivity and performance issues requires actionable insight into what is happening across the network. Fortinet brings AI assistance to SD-WAN operational workflows to help IT teams move more efficiently from investigation to corrective action.

FortiAI-Assist supports VPN diagnostics, network troubleshooting, and guided remediation. AI assistance in FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer simplifies alert triage, overlay preparation, and policy analysis, helping teams investigate reachability and path selection with current device information and historical analytics.

For example, when a branch experiences intermittent application access, engineers can use AI-assisted diagnostics to assess tunnel health, routing behavior, and relevant policies. Supported workflows allow administrators to review proposed fixes and authorize one-click execution, reducing manual effort while preserving operational control.

AI agents for SD-WAN further streamline operations by generating configurations, validating syntax, and creating policies through natural-language prompts. These capabilities help teams accelerate deployment preparation and reduce repetitive work, allowing engineers to focus on validating business requirements and maintaining consistent configurations across sites.

Improve Application Performance with Proactive Insights

Reliable connectivity requires continuous visibility into the conditions that affect application delivery. Latency, jitter, packet loss, and bandwidth utilization can degrade the user experience even when links remain available.

FortiAIOps combines predictive modeling, anomaly detection, and dynamic baselines with real-time monitoring of WAN service-level agreements (SLAs) to help IT teams identify emerging performance issues. These insights enable earlier investigation of congestion, abnormal behavior, and recurring SLA violations.

Teams can trace affected application traffic through the SD-WAN device and assess link conditions to isolate potential bottlenecks. Application-aware steering and failover select paths based on configured policies and SLAs, helping maintain a consistent application experience as network conditions change.

Together, contextual insights and policy-based path selection enable organizations to respond to performance issues more efficiently across distributed locations.

Strengthen Protection and Control AI Application Usage

GenAI adoption introduces new visibility and control requirements. IT teams need to understand which AI applications employees are using, distinguish approved services from shadow AI, and enforce consistent policies across the branch network. Unsanctioned AI tools can expose sensitive information, create compliance gaps, and introduce unmanaged third-party risk.

Fortinet AI-aware application control and shadow AI detection provide visibility into GenAI usage, helping teams identify unsanctioned applications and enforce granular, per-user controls. Integrated FortiGuard AI-Powered Security Services protect network traffic, while FortiAI-assisted policy reviews help identify redundant rules, unused policies, and potential security risks for correction by administrators.

Quantum computing poses a separate, long-term challenge for organizations that need to protect sensitive data over extended periods. Advances in quantum computing could render some current cryptographic methods vulnerable. In harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks, adversaries collect encrypted data today with the intention of decrypting it when the necessary capabilities become available.

Fortinet supports the long-term confidentiality of data in transit through quantum-safe tunnels. Hybrid key exchange combines classical and post-quantum algorithms to help defend against emerging threats while enabling a practical transition to post-quantum cryptography. These capabilities help organizations adapt their protection as application usage, AI governance requirements, and cryptographic risks evolve.

Conclusion

This campaign illustrates how BITTER combines native Windows tools with custom malware to establish and maintain access to targeted systems. The first infection chain uses ftp.exe, curl, scripts, and scheduled tasks without deploying a traditional malware executable, potentially reducing visibility for endpoint controls focused on executable files. The other two chains deliver PapRAT through LNK files and MSI installers, enabling system reconnaissance, file manipulation, secondary payload delivery, screenshot capture, and remote command execution.

PapRAT’s C++ and Rust implementations indicate continued investment in BITTER’s toolset. The Rust variant expands the implant’s command set from eight to eleven, adding PowerShell execution, a sleep directive, and a clean exit command. These changes underscore the importance of monitoring malicious behavior across scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity alongside detecting known malware signatures.

Organizations should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, particularly when delivered through unsolicited messages. Combining user awareness with controls that detect suspicious execution chains and outbound C2 traffic can help limit exposure to campaigns that blend legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware.

articles.title: What AI Cybercrime Exercises Reveal About Collective Defense
articles.context: As attackers accelerate their operations and obscure evidence available to defenders, those unresolved questions become harder to manage
articles.full_text:
AI-enabled cybercrime has increased pressure on the decisions that link detection to response. While security teams may recognize an attack, their organization may still be uncertain about who can authorize action, what information can be shared, or when to communicate with customers and partners. As attackers accelerate their operations and obscure evidence available to defenders, those unresolved questions become harder to manage.

That is a central lesson drawn from a series of tabletop exercises conducted by the AI-enabled Cybercrime Initiative, a collaboration among Fortinet, UC Berkeley’s Center for Long-Term Cybersecurity (CLTC), the Berkeley Risk and Security Lab (BRSL), and other partners.

My accompanying analysis with CLTC, “Who Decides How to Respond during a Cyber Crisis? What Three Tabletop Exercises Revealed About AI-Enabled Cybercrime,” examines the governance challenges that emerged from those sessions. From Fortinet’s perspective, those findings underscore why contributing to shared research matters: Improving collective defense requires understanding how organizations make decisions together and how attackers operate.

Connecting Research with Operational Experience

As a CLTC research partner, Fortinet supported the initiative’s launch and has contributed directly to its research and exercises. In Singapore, I helped lead the tabletop exercise alongside project lead Dr. Gil Baram and Helena Huang, associate research fellow in the executive deputy chairman’s office at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies. Practitioner involvement like this grounds academic research into the wider consequences of AI-enabled cybercrime in how incidents actually unfold.

Fortinet also helped bring the research to a wider audience. At RSAC 2025, Fortinet joined CLTC, BRSL, and Nanyang Technological University experts to discuss the initiative alongside threat intelligence from FortiGuard Labs. That exchange helped connect the scenarios being studied with observations of how criminals were adopting AI.

That combination of public sector, academic, and industry expertise helps participants examine problems that extend beyond any single organization’s visibility or authority. A security provider may hold evidence that a government needs. A business may depend on a supplier’s investigation to understand its own exposure. And importantly, decisions made by one participant can change the options available to everyone else.

This work also builds on Fortinet’s earlier participation in CLTC’s Cybersecurity Futures 2030 project. Across both efforts, scenario planning gives leaders a structured way to question assumptions and prepare for conditions their current plans may not adequately address.

By bringing these perspectives into the same scenarios, the initiative creates an opportunity to expose conflicting assumptions before an actual incident makes them consequential. The resulting lessons can inform organizations beyond those represented in the exercises.

What the Three Exercises Revealed

The progression through the exercises is instructive. Early discussions at Berkeley examined how AI could make phishing, impersonation, and reconnaissance more accessible. The Singapore event explored the implications for incident response and for disruptions across critical infrastructure. Operation Black Ice in Tel Aviv brought impersonation, supplier compromise, and ransomware together into a single crisis, testing decisions under competing pressures.

Across these sessions, participants often understood the threat but struggled to determine what action they could take. Three recurring problems deserve particular attention from security leaders:

First, consequential decisions arrived before reliable answers. At UC Berkeley, participants needed to advise clients while attribution remained unresolved. Similarly, in Singapore, pressure for public guidance preceded a clear understanding of the compromise. The practical challenge, therefore, is deciding what evidence is sufficient for a particular action and how to communicate uncertainty without creating confusion.

Second, response obligations collided. The Singapore scenario placed energy, transport, and water systems under pressure within the same response window. In Tel Aviv, legal authorization, board notification, and regulatory disclosure competed for attention. To address issues like these, playbooks need to account for simultaneous demands and establish how they will resolve competing priorities.

Third, information and authority were divided. In the UC Berkeley scenario, a private firm held forensic data while the government held the relevant authority to act. Participants encountered a circular dependency: Sharing required attribution, but attribution depended on sharing. That scenario illustrates how individually reasonable requirements can obstruct a collective response.

Of course, these were simulated incidents, and the findings should be understood in that context. Even so, the recurrence of similar difficulties across different jurisdictions gives leaders a useful basis for examining their own response arrangements.

Making Collaboration Work Under Pressure

The operational implication is clear: Threat intelligence delivers greater value when the people receiving it have the authority and established relationships to act. Improving detection speed should be paired with efforts to remove avoidable delays in escalation and coordination.

Organizations can begin by defining decision authority before an incident. Security, legal, communications, and executive teams should understand which decisions they own, which require consultation, and how to escalate disagreements. Those arrangements should be exercised when several urgent demands arrive together.

External coordination deserves similar attention. Partners should establish what information they can share during an investigation, how they will indicate their confidence in that information, and which channels will remain available if normal connections are interrupted. Exercises should then test whether those arrangements hold when a supplier is compromised or when several sectors are affected.

While AI-assisted detection and triage can help teams process information faster, leaders still need to determine how those outputs inform action and where human approval is required. Testing the relationship between technical capability and decision authority is an important part of making that investment effective. AI can compress the time between signal and decision, but accountability for that decision must remain with the people who have the authority to act.

Looking Ahead to Phase 2 with CLTC

Phase 1 provides a strong foundation for continued collaboration as Fortinet looks ahead to Phase 2 of the initiative with CLTC, beginning in 2027. It identified practical questions about how defenders can respond when attacks move faster than their established decision processes.

A valuable next step is to assess whether proposed improvements hold up under pressure. Can clearer decision authority reduce delays? Can partners share useful evidence even when attribution remains uncertain? Can AI-assisted analysis help leaders make timely decisions while preserving accountability? Phase 1 positions the broader cybersecurity community to answer them.

Fortinet’s contribution to this work reflects a responsibility that extends beyond individual customer environments. By participating in joint exercises and research, we can help translate operational experience into lessons that other defenders can apply. Continued collaboration with CLTC offers an opportunity to build on those lessons and strengthen the collective response to AI-enabled cybercrime.

Explore CLTC’s AI-Enabled Cybercrime Initiative and the research informing this collaboration.

articles.title: Building Cybersecurity Careers through Certification and Continuous Learning
articles.context: Fortinet’s 2026 report found that 91% of IT decision-makers prefer candidates with technology-focused certifications
articles.full_text:
Building a stronger cybersecurity workforce requires creating accessible opportunities for new talent while continuing to invest in experienced professionals. As AI reshapes cybersecurity, organizations need people who can protect the systems they rely on today, use AI to strengthen security capabilities, and develop the expertise to address emerging threats.

Fortinet’s 2026 Cybersecurity Skills Gap Global Research Report found that 71% of respondents believe the skills shortage creates additional cyber risks for their organizations, while 56% cited a lack of cybersecurity skills and trained IT or security staff as a cause of breaches.

Addressing that gap requires more than making training available. People need to know where to start, which skills to develop next, and how to demonstrate what they have learned. The Fortinet Network Security Expert (NSE) Certification Program provides that structure, helping learners build and validate skills as they enter the field, specialize, or prepare for greater responsibility.

Using Certification to Guide Career Development

Cybersecurity careers do not follow a single route. Some professionals begin with foundational IT skills and are preparing to enter the field. Others already work in IT or cybersecurity and want to advance or take on more complex responsibilities. Both need a clear way to identify relevant skills and build on what they already know.

The NSE Certification Program guides learners from cybersecurity fundamentals to advanced technical disciplines. Training and certification cover areas including secure networking, secure access service edge (SASE), cloud security, security operations, and operational technology (OT) security. Learners can select relevant certifications by considering their current knowledge, the responsibilities they want to take on, and the requirements for each credential.

Free self-paced lessons, instructor-led training, and hands-on learning give learners several ways to build their knowledge and prepare for certification. A defined certification goal helps turn a broad career ambition into a learning plan with specific skills to develop and requirements to meet.

Industry-recognized certifications provide a way to demonstrate knowledge and technical proficiency. Fortinet’s 2026 report found that 91% of IT decision-makers prefer candidates with technology-focused certifications. A relevant certification can help professionals convey their capabilities to employers, while hiring teams can weigh certifications alongside practical assessments and experience when evaluating candidates.

Connecting Training with Practical Experience

An effective learning plan links instruction to practical application. Those new to the field can start with networking and cybersecurity fundamentals, then pursue training tailored to a specific role. Hands-on labs offer a controlled environment to configure systems, investigate suspicious activity, and test decisions. Mentored projects and workplace assignments allow learners to apply those skills in an organizational context.

For individuals, progress can be measured through completed courses, demonstrated lab skills, and certifications earned. For employers and educators, those milestones can help identify development needs and connect training investments to specific responsibilities. Reviewing that progress also helps learners decide where to focus their next training or certification goal.

Developing Skills as Roles and Technologies Evolve

A cybersecurity career continues to evolve after someone earns an initial certification. Technologies change, and professionals often move into new areas of responsibility. Ongoing training and certification can support both reskilling and upskilling as those needs develop.

Reskilling prepares someone for a new role, such as an IT support professional moving into security operations. Upskilling builds on existing capabilities, such as a security analyst learning to investigate incidents across cloud environments. Both start by defining the role or responsibility and assessing the knowledge needed to perform it.

AI is another reason to keep learning. Fortinet’s 2026 report found that 63% of respondents expect a greater need for AI oversight and governance roles on cybersecurity teams over the next three years. Professionals must learn how AI changes their environments, evaluate the outputs of AI tools, and manage the security risks associated with their adoption.

Other areas also require specialized knowledge. Cloud security requires understanding access controls and how responsibilities are shared between providers and customers. OT security requires familiarity with industrial environments, where decisions must account for safety and operational continuity. Employers should tailor ongoing training and certification goals to the environments their teams protect and the responsibilities employees are preparing for.

Making Workforce Development a Shared Responsibility

Accessible training depends on support from the organizations that educate and employ cybersecurity professionals. Employers need to fund courses and certification exams, allocate time for learning, and provide opportunities to apply new skills. Educational institutions can partner with industry to align curricula with current needs, and government and community partners can expand access for people facing financial or other barriers.

Employers can also broaden access by assessing candidates based on the skills a role requires and recognizing experience gained through diverse educational and professional backgrounds. Internships, apprenticeships, and mentoring give students, career changers, veterans, and people from underrepresented communities opportunities to apply what they have learned and build experience.

Fortinet supports these efforts through the Fortinet Training Institute, including its certification program, academic partnerships, and education outreach initiatives. In June 2026, Fortinet announced that it had trained more than 1 million people in cybersecurity, achieving that goal ahead of its December 2026 target.

Continued progress depends on connecting education with opportunities to enter the workforce and advance within it. By investing in new talent and giving existing employees a clear way to develop and validate their skills, organizations can build the capabilities needed to address current security gaps and prepare for changing demands. The NSE Certification Program helps individuals and employers turn those development goals into practical next steps.

Explore the Fortinet NSE Certification Program to find training options, review certification requirements, and identify the next steps in your cybersecurity career or your team’s development.

For more detailed guidance on training and certifications aligned with specific cybersecurity work roles, explore Fortinet Education Pathways.

articles.title: Critical vulnerabilities in Fortinet products
articles.context: Fortinet have announced critical vulnerabilities in Fortinet products and are releasing critical security updates for a wide range of products
articles.full_text:
Fortinet have announced critical vulnerabilities in Fortinet products and are releasing critical security updates for a wide range of products. Fortinet are advising customers to complete the security updates as a priority.

This alert is intended for all organisations using Fortinet products.

Background

Fortinet are releasing critical security updates to a wide range of products. Fortinet have recommended customers implement the security updates as a prioirity.

The Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) is monitoring the situation but has no further details beyond Fortinet’s current public advice. Fortinet is expected to release more information 10 November 2026.

Fortinet has announced that multiple versions of FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator are affected.

A comprehensive list of affected products and fixed versions can be found here.

Fortinet have advised affected versions of FortiSASE have already had security updates applied automatically but FortiManager products may require manual updates.

ASD’s ACSC is currently not aware of active exploitation related to these vulnerabilities in Australia.

Mitigation advice

ASD’s ACSC advises individuals and organisations to:

Identify Fortinet products within their environments.

Apply available security updates.

Monitor and review Fortinet official guidance.

Continue to monitor Fortinet products for evidence of exploitation activity.

Where the relevant security updates are unable to be implemented immediately, Fortinet have recommended customer reduce exposure by:

Restricting administrative interfaces (HTTPS, SSH) to trusted IP addresses or disable them on external interfaces.

Ensuring FortiManager administration is not reachable from the internet.

Implementing strong credentials and mandating Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on user accounts.

Where to get help

Organisations that have been impacted, suspect impact or require advice and assistance can contact us via 1300 CYBER1 (1300 292 371), or at www.cyber.gov.au/submit-a-report.

articles.title: ZDI-26-772: Fortinet FortiSandbox Admin Profile Improper Handling of Exceptional Conditions Denial-of-Service Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to create a denial-of-service condition on affected installations of Fortinet FortiSandbox
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to create a denial-of-service condition on affected installations of Fortinet FortiSandbox. Authentication is required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of the users field. The issue results from the lack of proper handling of error conditions. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to create a denial-of-service condition on the system.

Additional Details

Fortinet has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://fortiguard.fortinet.com/psirt/FG-IR-26-176

Disclosure Timeline

2026-06-19 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-10-15 - Coordinated public release of advisory

2026-10-15 - Advisory Updated

Credit

Jason McFadyen of TrendAI Research

articles.title: ZDI-26-771: Fortinet FortiSandbox login_user_profile Hard-Coded Credentials Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to bypass authentication on affected installations of Fortinet FortiSandbox
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to bypass authentication on affected installations of Fortinet FortiSandbox. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the authentication mechanism. The issue results from the use of hard-coded credentials. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to bypass authentication on the system.

Additional Details

Fortinet has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://fortiguard.fortinet.com/psirt/FG-IR-26-185

Disclosure Timeline

2026-06-19 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-10-15 - Coordinated public release of advisory

2026-10-15 - Advisory Updated
